eic.name: English East India Company
eic.summary: A London joint-stock company chartered in 1600 to trade in Asia. By 1765 it collected the land revenue of Bengal and Bihar and kept its own army.

eic-diwani.name: Bengal under Company diwani
eic-diwani.summary: After 1765 the Company held the diwani (the right to collect revenue) for Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The Nawab kept the nizamat (justice and policing) in name only. Historians call this arrangement the "dual government".

bengal-nawabs.name: Nawabs of Bengal
bengal-nawabs.summary: The Mughal province of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. It was in practice independent under nawabs based at Murshidabad, and it was the richest province of the empire.

awadh.name: Nawabs of Awadh
awadh.summary: A Mughal successor state in the middle Ganges plain. Shuja-ud-Daula ruled from 1754, and his defeat at Buxar made Awadh a buffer state of the Company.

mughal.name: Mughal Empire
mughal.summary: By the 1740s the emperor in Delhi was sovereign in name, but his real power reached little beyond the capital region. Provincial governors and rival powers held the rest.

maratha-peshwa.name: Maratha Confederacy (Peshwa)
maratha-peshwa.summary: A confederacy based at Pune under the Peshwas. In the 1750s it was the strongest power on the subcontinent, until its defeat at Panipat in 1761.

marathas-nagpur.name: Bhonsles of Nagpur
marathas-nagpur.summary: A Maratha house based at Nagpur. Its armies raided Bengal from 1741, and in 1751 it took Orissa from the Nawab of Bengal.

rohillas.name: Rohillas
rohillas.summary: Afghan chiefs who took control of Rohilkhand, north-west of Awadh, in the 1740s.

hyderabad.name: Nizams of Hyderabad
hyderabad.summary: A Mughal successor state in the Deccan, independent in practice from 1724.

mysore.name: Kingdom of Mysore
mysore.summary: A Wodeyar kingdom in the southern Deccan. From 1761 the commander Haidar Ali held real power.

carnatic.name: Nawabs of the Carnatic (Arcot)
carnatic.summary: A Mughal successor state on the Coromandel coast. Rival claimants backed by the British and the French fought for it in the Carnatic Wars.

travancore.name: Travancore
travancore.summary: A kingdom in the far south-west, enlarged by Marthanda Varma in the 1740s.

french.name: French East India Company
french.summary: The main European rival of the British in the 1740s–1750s. Its headquarters was Pondicherry.

dutch.name: Dutch East India Company (VOC)
dutch.summary: The VOC, once the leading European trader in Asia. Its Bengal base was Chinsurah.

danish.name: Danish East India Company
danish.summary: A small Danish trading presence at Tranquebar (from 1620) and Serampore (from 1755).

portuguese.name: Portuguese Estado da Índia
portuguese.summary: The first European power in India. By the 18th century it held only Goa, Daman and Diu.

bengal-presidency.name: Bengal Presidency
bengal-presidency.summary: The largest and oldest British province, governed from Calcutta. In 1857 it covered Bengal, Bihar, Orissa and, until 1874, Assam. It was split in 1905, reunited in 1912, and partitioned between India and Pakistan in 1947.

madras-presidency.name: Madras Presidency
madras-presidency.summary: The southern presidency, governed from Madras (Fort St George). It was stable in extent through the Raj, apart from losing Ganjam and Koraput to Orissa in 1936.

bombay-presidency.name: Bombay Presidency
bombay-presidency.summary: The western presidency, governed from Bombay. It included Sind until 1936, and many small princely states were attached to it.

up.name: United Provinces

names.name: United Provinces of Agra and Oudh

up.summary: The upper Ganges plain, a heartland of the 1857 revolt. It began as the North-Western Provinces, absorbed Oudh in 1877, and was renamed the United Provinces in 1902.

oudh.name: Chief Commissionership of Oudh
oudh.summary: Annexed by Dalhousie in February 1856 on grounds of "misgovernment". The annexation was a major grievance in 1857, when Lucknow was besieged. It was merged with the North-Western Provinces in 1877.

punjab.name: Punjab
punjab.summary: Annexed in 1849 after the Anglo-Sikh wars. It became a major recruiting ground for the Indian Army, and it was partitioned in 1947.

nagpur-province.name: Nagpur Province
nagpur-province.summary: The Bhonsle kingdom of Nagpur, annexed by lapse in 1853. It was merged into the Central Provinces in 1861.

central-provinces.name: Central Provinces
central-provinces.summary: Formed in 1861 from Nagpur Province and the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories. Berar was attached in 1903.

berar.name: Berar (Hyderabad Assigned Districts)
berar.summary: Assigned by the Nizam of Hyderabad to the British in 1853 to pay for troops. It was formally still Hyderabad's, and from 1903 it was run as part of the Central Provinces.

assam.name: Assam
assam.summary: Separated from Bengal as a chief commissionership in 1874, with Sylhet attached. It was merged into Eastern Bengal and Assam from 1905 to 1912, and became a governor's province in 1921.

eastern-bengal-assam.name: Eastern Bengal and Assam
eastern-bengal-assam.summary: The province created by Curzon's partition of Bengal in 1905, with its capital at Dacca. It had a Muslim majority. Mass protest (the Swadeshi movement) forced the partition to be annulled in 1911.

bihar.name: Bihar
bihar.summary: Carved out of Bengal in 1912 as Bihar and Orissa, with its capital at Patna. Orissa was separated in 1936.

orissa.name: Orissa
orissa.summary: The first Indian province drawn on linguistic lines (1936), formed from Bihar and Orissa and the Oriya-speaking districts of Madras.

sind.name: Sind
sind.summary: Conquered in 1843 and governed as part of Bombay until it became a separate province in 1936.

nwfp.name: North-West Frontier Province
nwfp.summary: Separated from Punjab by Curzon in 1901 to manage the Afghan frontier. It was the base of Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgar movement.

baluchistan.name: British Baluchistan
baluchistan.summary: Built up from the Quetta lease (1876) and the districts ceded by Afghanistan at Gandamak (1879). It was a chief commissioner's province from 1887.

burma.name: Burma
burma.summary: Conquered in three wars (1824–1885) and governed as a province of British India until 1937, when it became a separate colony.

delhi.name: Delhi Province
delhi.summary: Separated from Punjab in 1912 after the capital moved from Calcutta. New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931.

ajmer-merwara.name: Ajmer-Merwara
ajmer-merwara.summary: A small British enclave among the Rajputana states, ceded by Sindhia in 1818.

coorg.name: Coorg
coorg.summary: A small hill kingdom annexed in 1834 and governed as a chief commissioner's province.

mysore-commission.name: Mysore (British commission)
mysore-commission.summary: The British took over Mysore's administration in 1831 and returned it to the Wodeyar dynasty in 1881 (the "rendition").

hyderabad-state.name: Hyderabad
hyderabad-state.summary: The largest and richest princely state, ruled by the Nizam. In 1948 India annexed it by force ("Operation Polo").

mysore-state.name: Mysore
mysore-state.summary: A princely state from 1881, after its rendition. It was a model "progressive" state, with Bangalore as its leading city.

jammu-kashmir.name: Jammu and Kashmir
jammu-kashmir.summary: Created by the Treaty of Amritsar (1846). Its Hindu ruler governed a Muslim-majority population, and its accession in October 1947 began the Kashmir dispute.

baroda.name: Baroda
baroda.summary: The Gaekwad's state in Gujarat, one of the five largest gun-salute states.

gwalior.name: Gwalior
gwalior.summary: The Sindhia's state. Its army joined the rebels in 1857, and Rani Lakshmibai died in battle near Gwalior.

travancore-state.name: Travancore
travancore-state.summary: A princely state in the far south, known for high literacy. The 1936 Temple Entry Proclamation opened its temples to all castes.

cochin-state.name: Cochin
cochin-state.summary: A princely state on the Malabar coast.

rajputana-states.name: Rajputana Agency states
rajputana-states.summary: About 20 Rajput and other states (Jaipur, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Bikaner and others) under a British political agent.

central-india-states.name: Central India Agency states
central-india-states.summary: Indore, Bhopal, Rewa and dozens of smaller states and estates.

western-india-states.name: Western India States
western-india-states.summary: Junagadh, Nawanagar, Bhavnagar, Cutch and over 200 smaller states and talukas in Gujarat. Gandhi's birthplace, Porbandar, was one of them.

deccan-states.name: Bombay and Deccan states
deccan-states.summary: Kolhapur, Sangli, Bhor and other states attached to the Bombay Presidency.

orissa-states.name: Orissa feudatory states
orissa-states.summary: Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar and about 24 other states attached to Bengal, later Bihar and Orissa.

chhattisgarh-states.name: Chhattisgarh feudatory states
chhattisgarh-states.summary: Bastar, Surguja and about 13 other states attached to the Central Provinces.

punjab-states.name: Punjab and Simla Hill states
punjab-states.summary: The Phulkian states (Patiala, Nabha, Jind), Kapurthala, and the hill states around Simla.

eastern-states.name: Eastern states
eastern-states.summary: Cooch Behar, Tripura, Manipur and the Khasi states.

sikkim.name: Sikkim
sikkim.summary: A Himalayan kingdom under British protection from 1861.

bahawalpur.name: Bahawalpur
bahawalpur.summary: A large princely state on the Sutlej. It acceded to Pakistan in 1947.

khairpur.name: Khairpur
khairpur.summary: A princely state in Sind ruled by the Talpur Mirs.

baluchistan-states.name: Baluchistan states
baluchistan-states.summary: The Khanate of Kalat and its feudatories, Kharan, Las Bela and Makran.

frontier-states.name: Frontier states
frontier-states.summary: Swat, Dir and Chitral, under the Malakand political agency.

shan-states.name: Shan States
shan-states.summary: Shan principalities, tributary to the Burmese crown until 1885 and then under British protection.

tribal-areas.name: Tribal areas
tribal-areas.summary: Pashtun and Baloch tribal territories on the Afghan frontier. They were controlled through political agents, subsidies and punitive expeditions rather than direct administration.

kingdom-of-burma.name: Kingdom of Burma (Konbaung)
kingdom-of-burma.summary: The independent Burmese kingdom at Mandalay, conquered in the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885).

afghanistan.name: Emirate of Afghanistan
afghanistan.summary: Ceded Pishin and Sibi to the British by the Treaty of Gandamak (1879).

oman.name: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman
oman.summary: Held the port of Gwadar on the Makran coast from 1783 until it sold it to Pakistan in 1958.

dominion-india.name: Dominion of India
dominion-india.summary: Independent from 15 August 1947 under the Indian Independence Act. Most princely states acceded to it, a few (Hyderabad, Junagadh, Kashmir) only after crises.

dominion-pakistan.name: Dominion of Pakistan
dominion-pakistan.summary: Created on 14–15 August 1947 in two wings, West and East (East Bengal), separated by about 1,600 km of India.

keyframes.note: On the eve of the revolt. Company territory has reached its greatest extent: Dalhousie has annexed Punjab (1849), Pegu (1852), Nagpur and Jhansi (by lapse, 1853–54) and Oudh (1856). The princely states cover about two-fifths of the subcontinent.
After its recapture, Delhi is moved from the North-Western Provinces to Punjab as punishment.
Nagpur Province and the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories are merged into the new Central Provinces.
Sambalpur is transferred from Bengal to the Central Provinces.
Assam is separated from Bengal as a chief commissionership. Sylhet, a Bengali-speaking district, is attached to it, a decision that shaped the 1947 referendum.
Oudh is merged with the North-Western Provinces under a single lieutenant-governor.
In the Treaty of Gandamak, during the Second Anglo-Afghan War, Afghanistan cedes Pishin and Sibi.
The "rendition" of Mysore. After fifty years of British administration, Mysore is returned to its Wodeyar ruler.
After the Third Anglo-Burmese War, Upper Burma is annexed. King Thibaw is exiled to Ratnagiri in India.
British Baluchistan is constituted. Quetta, leased from the Khan of Kalat since 1876, becomes its seat.
The Zhob and Loralai tribal country is brought under the Baluchistan Agency.
Chagai and Nushki are leased from Kalat for the railway towards Persia.
Curzon separates the North-West Frontier Province from Punjab to manage the Afghan border directly.
Berar, leased in perpetuity from the Nizam in 1902, is attached to the Central Provinces.
Curzon's partition of Bengal. Eastern Bengal and Assam is formed with its capital at Dacca. Western Bengal keeps Bihar and Orissa, and gains Sambalpur.

The partition is annulled, as announced at the Delhi Durbar of December 1911. Bengal is reunited; Bihar and Orissa becomes a new province; Assam is restored; and Delhi becomes the new capital as its own province.
Two new provinces. Orissa is formed on linguistic lines, and Sind is separated from Bombay.

Independence and Partition. The British provinces are divided between the Dominions of India and Pakistan; Punjab and Bengal are split along the Radcliffe Line, and Sylhet joins East Bengal by referendum. Princely states are shown as they stood: most had acceded to India, some to Pakistan, while Hyderabad, Junagadh and Kashmir were still in dispute. Borders here follow the present-day boundary, which closely tracks the Radcliffe Line.

places.name: Calcutta
places.why: Capital of British India until 1911 and the centre of the Bengal Renaissance and early nationalism. It saw the Great Calcutta Killings of 1946.

places.name: Delhi
places.why: The Mughal capital, seized by the rebels in 1857 and retaken by siege. It hosted the imperial durbars and became the capital in 1911 (New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931).

places.name: Simla
places.why: The summer capital of the Raj, where the government moved each year to escape the heat of the plains.

places.name: Bombay
places.why: The commercial capital, where the Congress was founded in 1885, Quit India was launched in 1942 and the Navy mutinied in 1946.

places.name: Lahore
places.why: Capital of Punjab. It saw the 1929 Purna Swaraj resolution, the 1931 hanging of Bhagat Singh and the 1940 Lahore Resolution.

places.name: Karachi
places.why: Sind's port and Pakistan's first capital.

places.name: Dacca
places.why: Capital of Eastern Bengal and Assam (1905–1912), where the Muslim League was founded in 1906.

places.name: Rangoon
places.why: Capital of British Burma. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, died in exile here in 1862.

places.name: Mandalay
places.why: The royal capital of Burma, taken in 1885. Tilak and Bose were later imprisoned here.

places.name: Barrackpore
places.why: The cantonment where Mangal Pandey attacked his officers in March 1857.

places.name: Meerut
places.why: The 1857 revolt began here on 10 May, when sepoys freed their jailed comrades and marched on Delhi.

places.name: Cawnpore
places.why: Nana Sahib's siege of the British entrenchment here in 1857 ended in the Satichaura and Bibighar massacres, followed by savage British reprisals.

places.name: Lucknow
places.why: The capital of Oudh. Its Residency was besieged for months in 1857. The Congress and League concluded the Lucknow Pact here in 1916.

places.name: Jhansi
places.why: The state of Rani Lakshmibai, annexed by lapse in 1854 and stormed by Hugh Rose in April 1858.

places.name: Kalpi
places.why: The rebel base on the Yamuna where Lakshmibai and Tatya Tope regrouped in May 1858.

places.name: Gwalior
places.why: Rebels seized the fort in June 1858, and Lakshmibai died in battle nearby.

places.name: Allahabad
places.why: Where Queen Victoria's proclamation transferring India to the Crown was read in 1858. It was also the Nehru family home, Anand Bhavan.

places.name: Aligarh
places.why: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College here in 1875.

places.name: Krishnanagar
places.why: A centre of the 1859–60 indigo revolt in Nadia.

places.name: Ranchi
places.why: Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (the great tumult) in the Munda country around Ranchi, 1899–1900. He died in Ranchi jail.

places.name: Surat
places.why: Where the Congress split into Moderates and Extremists in 1907.

places.name: Poona
places.why: Tilak's city. Gandhi was held in its Yeravda prison, where the Poona Pact was signed in 1932.

places.name: Porbandar
places.why: Gandhi's birthplace (1869), a small Kathiawar princely state.

places.name: Motihari (Champaran)
places.why: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India (1917), on behalf of indigo cultivators.

places.name: Nadiad (Kheda)
places.why: Centre of the 1918 Kheda satyagraha against revenue collection after crop failure.

places.name: Sabarmati Ashram
places.why: Gandhi's base from 1917, and the starting point of the Salt March.

places.name: Amritsar
places.why: Jallianwala Bagh, where Dyer's troops fired on a crowd in April 1919.

places.name: Nagpur
places.why: Capital of the Central Provinces. The 1920 Congress session here adopted non-cooperation.

places.name: Tirurangadi
places.why: A centre of the 1921 Malabar (Mappila) rebellion.

places.name: Chauri Chaura
places.why: Where a crowd burned a police station in 1922, after which Gandhi called off non-cooperation.

places.name: Bardoli
places.why: Vallabhbhai Patel's 1928 no-tax campaign here earned him the title "Sardar".

places.name: Kakori
places.why: Where HRA revolutionaries robbed a government train in 1925.

places.name: Dandi
places.why: The end of the Salt March, where Gandhi picked up salt on 6 April 1930.

places.name: Dharasana
places.why: Salt works where non-violent volunteers were beaten in May 1930. Webb Miller's report reached the world.

places.name: Chittagong
places.why: Surya Sen's revolutionaries raided the armouries here in April 1930.

places.name: Peshawar
places.why: Capital of the NWFP. Troops fired on Khudai Khidmatgar protesters at the Qissa Khwani Bazaar in 1930.

places.name: Sevagram (Wardha)
places.why: Gandhi's ashram from 1936, and the de facto headquarters of the Congress in the late 1930s.

places.name: Imphal
places.why: Capital of Manipur state. Japanese and INA forces besieged it in 1944 and were defeated, alongside Kohima.

places.name: Noakhali
places.why: Scene of communal violence in October 1946. Gandhi walked village to village here for four months.

places.name: Port Blair
places.why: The penal settlement on the Andamans, set up after 1857. Its Cellular Jail held revolutionaries.

places.name: Quetta
places.why: A frontier garrison and capital of British Baluchistan. It was destroyed by an earthquake in 1935.

places.name: Pondicherry
places.why: Capital of French India throughout the Raj. It was transferred to India in 1954.

control.note: Restored to France after the Napoleonic Wars

places.name: Chandernagore
places.why: A French enclave beside Calcutta, sometimes a refuge for Bengali revolutionaries.

places.name: Goa
places.why: Capital of Portuguese India. It stayed Portuguese until India took it in 1961.

events.name: Mangal Pandey's attack at Barrackpore
events.summary: A sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry attacks his officers. Unrest had been growing over cartridges rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat. He is hanged on 8 April.

events.name: Meerut uprising
events.summary: Sepoys mutiny, free 85 comrades jailed for refusing the cartridges, kill British officers and civilians, and ride for Delhi.

events.name: Revolt of 1857
events.summary: A rising of sepoys across the Bengal Army, joined by dispossessed rulers, landholders and peasants across the Ganges plain and central India. It is crushed with mass reprisals by mid-1858.
events.why: It ended Company rule and the Mughal dynasty. After it the Raj stopped annexing princely states and reorganised the army on "martial race" lines. Its name is still contested: "Mutiny" in colonial accounts, the "First War of Independence" in V. D. Savarkar's 1909 book and in later nationalist usage.

events.name: Rebels take Delhi
events.summary: The Meerut sepoys reach Delhi and proclaim the aged Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar leader of the revolt.
events.why: The revolt gains a symbol of legitimacy, the Mughal crown.

events.name: Siege of Cawnpore
events.summary: Nana Sahib's forces besiege the British entrenchment, which surrenders on 25 June. The evacuees are massacred at Satichaura Ghat, and in July the women and children held at the Bibighar are killed. British reprisals follow.

events.name: Siege of the Lucknow Residency
events.summary: The British Residency is besieged for nearly five months. It is relieved, then evacuated in November. Begum Hazrat Mahal leads the resistance in Oudh until Lucknow falls in March 1858.

events.name: Delhi recaptured
events.summary: After a long siege, British forces storm the city. The emperor surrenders and his sons are shot. The city is sacked and many residents are killed or expelled.

events.name: Storming of Jhansi
events.summary: Hugh Rose takes Jhansi. Rani Lakshmibai escapes by night to Kalpi.

events.name: Death of Rani Lakshmibai
events.summary: The Rani of Jhansi is killed fighting British cavalry near Gwalior.
events.why: She became the best-remembered figure of 1857, both as a symbol and in later nationalist memory.

events.name: Queen's Proclamation: Crown takes over
events.summary: Under the Government of India Act 1858, the Company's rule passes to the Crown. Canning, now the first Viceroy, reads the Queen's proclamation at Allahabad. It promises religious non-interference and an end to annexation.
events.why: The Raj, direct British Crown rule, begins.

events.name: Indigo revolt
events.summary: Bengal ryots (cultivators) refuse to grow indigo for European planters. The play Nil Darpan publicises their cause.

events.name: Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College founded
events.summary: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founds a college to give Muslims Western education. It later becomes Aligarh Muslim University.

events.name: Great Famine of 1876–78
events.summary: Drought across the Deccan and south. Grain exports continued, and relief was kept deliberately limited.
events.why: The famine became central to nationalist critiques of the economics of British rule.

figures.label: Deaths
figures.note: Estimates vary by method and region.

events.name: Delhi Durbar of 1877
events.summary: Lytton proclaims Queen Victoria Empress of India in a vast imperial assembly, during the famine.

events.name: Ilbert Bill controversy
events.summary: A bill to let Indian judges try Europeans provokes a furious European backlash and is diluted.
events.why: The affair showed educated Indians how far racial privilege went, and fed the push for an all-India body.

events.name: Mandalay taken
events.summary: The Third Anglo-Burmese War ends in days. King Thibaw is deposed and exiled to India.

events.name: Indian National Congress founded
events.summary: Seventy-two delegates meet in Bombay for the first session of the Indian National Congress.

events.name: Birsa Munda's Ulgulan
events.summary: Munda adivasis rise against landlords, moneylenders and colonial land law. Birsa dies in Ranchi jail in June 1900.
events.why: The rising led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908, which protected adivasi land.

events.name: Swadeshi movement
events.summary: Boycott of British goods, bonfires of foreign cloth, national schools, and "Bande Mataram" as a rallying cry.

events.name: Partition of Bengal
events.summary: Curzon splits Bengal. The stated reason is administrative efficiency, but it was widely seen as a way to divide Bengali Hindus and Muslims.
events.why: It triggered the Swadeshi movement, the first mass nationalist campaign, and was annulled in 1911.

events.name: All-India Muslim League founded
events.summary: Founded at Dacca by Muslim notables to represent Muslim political interests.

events.name: Surat split
events.summary: The Congress splits between Moderates (Gokhale) and Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal).

events.name: Morley–Minto reforms
events.summary: Expanded legislative councils with separate electorates for Muslims.
events.why: Separate electorates became a lasting and contested feature of Indian politics.

events.name: Delhi Durbar of 1911
events.summary: George V announces that the capital will move from Calcutta to Delhi and that Bengal's partition is annulled.

events.name: Gandhi returns to India
events.summary: After 21 years in South Africa, Gandhi lands at Bombay.

events.name: Lucknow Pact
events.summary: The Congress and the Muslim League agree on joint demands, accepting separate electorates.

events.name: Champaran Satyagraha
events.summary: Gandhi goes to Champaran on behalf of tenants forced to grow indigo, defies an order to leave, and wins an inquiry.

events.name: Kheda Satyagraha
events.summary: Peasants refuse to pay land revenue after crop failure. Patel joins Gandhi.

events.name: Rowlatt Act and satyagraha
events.summary: Wartime powers of detention without trial are extended into peacetime. Gandhi calls a nationwide hartal (general strike), the first all-India protest.

events.name: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
events.summary: Brigadier-General Dyer's troops fire without warning on an unarmed crowd in a walled garden on Baisakhi, until their ammunition runs low.
events.why: It turned moderates against the Raj. Tagore returned his knighthood, and Gandhi moved to non-cooperation.

figures.label: Killed
figures.note: The official Hunter Committee figure is 379. The Congress inquiry estimated about 1,000.

events.name: Government of India Act 1919
events.summary: Introduces "dyarchy", under which some provincial subjects are handed to elected Indian ministers.

events.name: Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements
events.summary: Boycott of councils, courts, schools and foreign cloth, joined with the Khilafat cause. It was the first mass movement under Gandhi.

events.name: Malabar rebellion
events.summary: A Mappila rising against the British and landlords, rooted in Khilafat and agrarian grievances. It was crushed by martial law. Its character is still contested: agrarian revolt, anti-colonial war, or communal violence.

events.name: Chauri Chaura
events.summary: After police fire on protesters, a crowd burns the police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi suspends non-cooperation.

events.name: Kakori train action
events.summary: Hindustan Republican Association revolutionaries seize government money from a train. Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan and others are later hanged.

events.name: Bardoli Satyagraha
events.summary: A successful no-tax campaign against a revenue increase, led by Vallabhbhai Patel.

events.name: Simon Commission protests
events.summary: An all-white commission on constitutional reform is met with "Simon Go Back". Lala Lajpat Rai is beaten by police at Lahore and dies weeks later.

events.name: Central Assembly bombing
events.summary: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt throw harmless bombs and leaflets in the Assembly and court arrest.

events.name: Purna Swaraj resolution
events.summary: At Lahore, under Nehru's presidency, the Congress declares complete independence its goal, and the flag is raised on the banks of the Ravi. 26 January 1930 is marked as Independence Day.

events.name: Salt March
events.summary: Gandhi and 78 followers walk about 385 km from Sabarmati to Dandi and break the salt law. Civil disobedience spreads across India.
events.why: A tax on something everyone needed made the injustice of the Raj easy to grasp everywhere, and the march was covered by the world's press.

events.name: Chittagong armoury raid
events.summary: Surya Sen's Indian Republican Army seizes the police and auxiliary armouries.

events.name: Qissa Khwani Bazaar massacre
events.summary: Troops fire on non-violent Khudai Khidmatgar protesters. Garhwali soldiers refuse orders to shoot.

figures.label: Killed
figures.note: The official figure was about 20. Nationalist estimates ran to several hundred.

events.name: Dharasana Satyagraha
events.summary: Volunteers led by Sarojini Naidu march on the salt works and are beaten by police, column by column.

events.name: Gandhi–Irwin Pact
events.summary: Civil disobedience is suspended in return for the release of prisoners. Gandhi attends the Second Round Table Conference.

events.name: Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev hanged
events.summary: The three are executed at Lahore jail for the 1928 killing of police officer J. P. Saunders.

events.name: Poona Pact
events.summary: Gandhi fasts against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Ambedkar agrees to reserved seats within joint electorates.
events.why: The pact is still debated: a coerced bargain, or an act of unity?

events.name: Government of India Act 1935
events.summary: Grants provincial autonomy and plans a federation including the princely states. The federation never comes into being.

events.name: Provincial elections of 1937
events.summary: The Congress wins majorities in most provinces and forms ministries. The Muslim League does poorly.

events.name: Lahore Resolution
events.summary: The Muslim League calls for "independent states" in the Muslim-majority regions.

events.name: Quit India movement
events.summary: At Gowalia Tank, Gandhi calls on the British to "Quit India": "Do or die". The leadership is jailed within hours, and a leaderless mass rising follows. It is crushed by force.

events.name: Bengal famine of 1943
events.summary: Wartime policy, the loss of Burmese rice, hoarding and administrative failure produce famine in Bengal.
events.why: The share of blame between wartime policy and other causes is still argued over.

figures.label: Deaths
figures.note: Estimates range from about 2.1 million to about 3 million.

events.name: Imphal and Kohima
events.summary: The Japanese invasion of India, with units of Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army, is defeated.

events.name: INA trials at the Red Fort
events.summary: Courts-martial of INA officers spark mass sympathy across India. Sentences are commuted.

events.name: Royal Indian Navy mutiny
events.summary: Ratings strike and mutiny in Bombay and Karachi. The episode shook British confidence in the armed forces.

events.name: Direct Action Day
events.summary: The Muslim League's call for "direct action" is followed by days of communal killing in Calcutta.

figures.label: Killed
figures.note: At least 4,000 dead. Some estimates are much higher.

events.name: Noakhali riots and Gandhi's walk
events.summary: Organised attacks on Hindus in Noakhali. Gandhi spends four months walking through the district.

events.name: Mountbatten Plan
events.summary: Partition and early independence are announced. The date is brought forward to August 1947.

events.name: Independence and Partition
events.summary: India and Pakistan become independent dominions. Nehru speaks of a "tryst with destiny". Gandhi is in Calcutta, fasting against the violence. The Radcliffe boundaries are published on 17 August.
events.why: The end of the Raj, and one of the largest forced migrations in history.

figures.label: Deaths in Partition violence
figures.note: Estimates vary by an order of magnitude.

people.name: Bhagat Singh
people.summary: A socialist revolutionary. He was involved in the killing of J. P. Saunders to avenge Lajpat Rai, and in the Assembly bombing. His trial and execution at 23 made him a national hero.

perspectives.text: Gandhi condemned the violence and did not make his commutation a condition of the Irwin pact. Many criticised him for this at the time.

itinerary.note: Bombs in the Central Assembly; courts arrest

people.name: M. K. Gandhi
people.summary: A lawyer from Porbandar who developed satyagraha (non-violent resistance) in South Africa. From 1919 he turned the Congress into a mass movement through non-cooperation, the Salt March and Quit India. He was assassinated in January 1948.

perspectives.text: The "Father of the Nation", whose non-violent mass politics broke the moral authority of the Raj.
A defender of the caste order in reformed form. His Poona fast forced Ambedkar to give up separate electorates.
He mobilised peasants but kept movements within limits acceptable to Indian propertied classes. He called off struggles, as after Chauri Chaura, when they went beyond his control.

itinerary.note: Sets out on the Salt March
Arrested near Dandi and taken to Yeravda
Sails for the Round Table Conference in London
Returns to a city in riots

people.name: Rani Lakshmibai
people.role: Rani of Jhansi, rebel leader of 1857
people.summary: Regent of Jhansi, whose adopted heir was refused recognition under the doctrine of lapse in 1854. She led Jhansi's resistance in 1858 and died fighting at Gwalior.

perspectives.text: First blamed for the killing of Jhansi's Europeans, though the evidence is weak. Hugh Rose called her the most dangerous rebel leader.
A symbol of resistance, as in Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's poem "Khoob ladi mardani".

itinerary.note: Takes charge of Jhansi after the garrison revolts

people.name: Subhas Chandra Bose
people.role: Congress president; leader of the Indian National Army
people.summary: Twice Congress president (1938, 1939). He broke with Gandhi, escaped house arrest in 1941, and sought Axis help. He led the Azad Hind government and the INA from Singapore and Rangoon.

perspectives.text: "Netaji", a revolutionary patriot whose INA hastened the end of British rule.
His alliance with Nazi Germany and imperial Japan remains a point of serious criticism.

itinerary.note: Leaves Rangoon as the British advance

people.name: Mangal Pandey
people.summary: Attacked his officers at Barrackpore in March 1857 and was hanged. A symbol of the revolt.

people.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
people.summary: Proclaimed leader of the revolt in 1857, tried, and exiled to Rangoon. A noted Urdu poet.

people.name: Nana Sahib
people.role: Adopted heir of the last Peshwa
people.summary: Led the rebels at Cawnpore and disappeared into Nepal in 1859.

people.name: Begum Hazrat Mahal
people.summary: Led resistance in Lucknow in 1857–58 in the name of her son. She died in exile in Kathmandu.

people.name: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
people.summary: Founded the Aligarh college to bring Muslims modern education.

people.name: Birsa Munda
people.summary: Led the Ulgulan of 1899–1900 and died in Ranchi jail aged 25. Revered as 'Dharti Aaba'.

people.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
people.summary: "Swaraj is my birthright." He was jailed in Mandalay from 1908 to 1914.

people.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
people.summary: A Congressman who brokered the Lucknow Pact. He later led the League's demand for Pakistan and became its first Governor-General.

people.name: Vallabhbhai Patel
people.summary: Led Kheda and Bardoli. As Home Minister after 1947 he oversaw the integration of the princely states.

people.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
people.summary: Congress president at Lahore in 1929 and India's first Prime Minister.

people.name: B. R. Ambedkar
people.summary: A jurist and anti-caste leader who signed the Poona Pact. He later chaired the drafting of India's constitution.

people.name: Lala Lajpat Rai
people.summary: Died after a police lathi-charge at a Simon Commission protest.

people.name: Ram Prasad Bismil
people.summary: Hanged for the Kakori action.

people.name: Surya Sen
people.summary: Led the Chittagong raid and was hanged in 1934.

people.name: Abdul Ghaffar Khan
people.summary: "Frontier Gandhi", who led a non-violent Pashtun movement allied with the Congress.

people.name: Sarojini Naidu
people.summary: The first Indian woman to be Congress president (1925). She led the Dharasana raid.

stories.title: The Raj in twelve moments
stories.subtitle: From the revolt of 1857 to independence and Partition

steps.title: Meerut, 10 May 1857
steps.text: Sepoys at Meerut revolt over cartridges, faith and pay, and ride through the night to Delhi. Within weeks the Ganges plain is aflame. Pink is Company territory; yellow is the princely states.

steps.title: The Rani's last stand
steps.text: Follow Lakshmibai from Jhansi to Kalpi to Gwalior. By mid-1858 the revolt is crushed, with reprisals that left deep scars.

steps.title: The Crown takes over
steps.text: The Company is abolished, and the Queen's proclamation promises an end to annexations. From now on the map changes by reorganisation, not conquest, except at the edges.

steps.title: Seventy-two delegates
steps.text: The Indian National Congress meets for the first time, in Bombay. It is a moderate, petitioning body for now.

steps.title: Empire at the edges
steps.text: Upper Burma is annexed in 1885–86. Watch the Baluchistan frontier fill in too. On the scale below, the second row shows each viceroy's term.

steps.title: Bengal divided
steps.text: Curzon cuts Bengal in two. A new deep-pink province appears in the east, and Swadeshi boycotts erupt. In 1911 the partition is reversed and the capital leaves Calcutta for Delhi.

steps.title: Jallianwala Bagh
steps.text: A walled garden in Amritsar becomes the place where moderate loyalty to the Raj ends. The official death toll and the Congress estimate are still hundreds apart.

steps.title: The Salt March
steps.text: Press play. Gandhi walks about 385 km from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days, and civil disobedience follows across India.

steps.title: New provinces
steps.text: Orissa and Sind become provinces. Burma will leave British India in 1937.

steps.title: Quit India
steps.text: "Do or die." The leadership is jailed overnight, and a leaderless rising follows.

steps.title: Famine in Bengal
steps.text: Millions die in a man-made famine in the middle of the war.

steps.title: Freedom, and Partition
steps.text: Two dominions, India and Pakistan. The princely states (still yellow) must choose. Partition uproots between ten and twenty million people.
